followUps:
Use -E to stop after preprocessing, -S to stop after compilation (assembly), and -c to stop after assembling (an object file).

Example: g++ -E main.cpp -o main.ii gives the expanded text, -S gives main.s, -c gives main.o. With no flag, all four stages run including linking. Use -E to see what macros and includes produced, and -S to inspect the generated assembly.

Name mangling is the compiler encoding a function's namespace, class and parameter types into its symbol name, so that overloads get different names in the object file.

The linker only knows flat symbol names. In C++ you can have void f(int) and void f(double); they become something like _Z1fi and _Z1fd. Mangling also makes a signature mismatch show up as an undefined reference. Use nm -C or c++filt to turn them back into readable names.

-flto (link-time optimization) keeps the compiler's intermediate form in the object files so the optimizer can see the whole program at link time, not one .cpp at a time.

That lets it inline a function from util.cpp into main.cpp and drop unused code across files. Example: a tiny getter defined in another .cpp can be inlined with LTO but not without it. The costs are slower links and more memory used during the link step.

code.title: Declaration vs definition

followUps:
It is a definition: at namespace scope, int x; creates the variable and reserves storage, and it is zero-initialized because it has static storage.

To only declare it, write extern int x;. That is why putting int x; in a header included by two .cpp files gives a multiple-definition link error: each file then defines its own x. (Inside a class, int x; is a member declaration, a different situation.)

A pointer has a fixed size no matter what it points to, but an object needs the compiler to know how many bytes it takes and what members it has.

With struct Node; alone, Node* p; is fine because a pointer is just an address (8 bytes on 64-bit). Node n; or sizeof(Node) fails because the size is unknown. You also cannot use p->val until the full definition is visible. This is how headers avoid including each other.

With a static library (.a), the linker only pulls in the members that satisfy symbols it currently needs, scanning left to right, so a library listed before the objects that use it can be skipped.

Example: g++ -lfoo main.o fails with undefined references, while g++ main.o -lfoo works. The linker sees main.o first, notes it needs foo(), then finds it in libfoo. If library A needs symbols from library B, list A before B.

extern "C" tells the compiler to give a function a plain C symbol name, without C++ name mangling.

C code has no overloads, so a C library exports add, not _Z3addii. If a C++ file declares it without extern "C", it asks the linker for the mangled name and gets an undefined reference. Headers shared by both languages wrap declarations in #ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { ... } #endif.

#pragma once is shorter and cannot have a name typo, but it is not in the standard; include guards are fully portable.

Guards: you must pick a unique macro name (copy-pasted names cause silently skipped headers), but they work everywhere. #pragma once: one line, and compilers can skip re-reading the file. Its weak spot is when the same file is reachable by different paths (copies, symlinks, odd network drives). In practice GCC, Clang and MSVC all support it well.

Since C++17, inline on a function or variable mainly means "multiple identical definitions across translation units are allowed and merged"; it is no longer a request to expand the code at the call site.

That is why you can put inline int maxConn = 100; or a small function body in a header without a multiple-definition link error. The compiler decides on its own whether to actually inline calls, so inline is not a speed hint.

code.title: Fundamental type sizes on this platform

followUps:
int_fast32_t is the type the platform thinks is fastest with at least 32 bits, so use it when you need a minimum range and care about speed more than exact size.

On x86-64 Linux glibc it is actually 8 bytes (long), because 64-bit arithmetic avoids extra work, while int32_t is exactly 4. That makes it a poor fit for arrays or file formats, where memory or layout matters. Use int32_t for exact layout, int_fast32_t for loop counters.

bool is at least 1 byte because every object must have its own address, and addresses point to bytes, not bits.

So sizeof(bool) is 1 on common platforms, even though it only holds true or false. Bit-level packing would need shifting and masking on every access. When you need real bits, use std::bitset<N> or std::vector<bool>, which pack 8 values per byte but return proxy objects instead of real references.

code.title: Two's complement and the int8_t range

followUps:
Do the negation in a wider or unsigned type: the magnitude of INT_MIN (2147483648) fits in unsigned int or long long even though it does not fit in int.

unsigned mag(int x) {
    return x < 0 ? 0u - (unsigned)x : (unsigned)x;
}
// mag(INT_MIN) == 2147483648u

Unsigned wrap-around is well defined, so 0u - 2147483648u gives 2147483648u. Time and space are O(1).

Since C++20, right-shifting a negative number is an arithmetic shift: the sign bit is copied in, so the result stays negative and the shift rounds toward minus infinity.

Example: -8 >> 1 is -4, and -1 >> 5 is still -1. Before C++20 this was implementation-defined, though nearly all compilers did the same. Left-shifting a negative value was undefined before C++20; shifting by a count that is negative or at least the bit width is still undefined.

code.title: Signed vs unsigned overflow and safe checks

followUps:
Any check that performs the overflowing addition first and tests afterwards is unsafe, because the compiler may assume the addition never overflowed and remove the test.

int sum = a + b;
if (sum < a) { /* overflow detected? */ }

For b > 0 the compiler reasons that a + b < a is impossible without overflow, so it may delete the branch. Safe versions: test before adding (a > INT_MAX - b), use __builtin_add_overflow, or do the math in long long.

Use unsigned types for bit patterns, masks, hashes and modular arithmetic, where wrap-around is what you want and defined behavior is guaranteed.

Example: a hash h = h * 31 + c on uint32_t wraps predictably on every platform. Do not use unsigned just because a value "cannot be negative": size_t i = 0; i-- wraps to a huge number, and i >= 0 is always true, which creates endless loops. For counts and indices that you subtract from, prefer a signed type.

code.title: Usual arithmetic conversions and their bugs

followUps:
It is int, with the value 98: 'a' is a char, which is promoted to int before the addition (97 + 1 = 98).

That is why std::cout << 'a' + 1 prints 98 and not b. To get a char back, cast it: static_cast<char>('a' + 1) is 'b'. The same promotion happens for short and bool in any arithmetic.

std::cmp_less(a, b) (C++20, in <utility>) compares the real mathematical values of two integers even when one is signed and the other unsigned.

With the normal operator, -1 < 1u is false because -1 converts to 4294967295u. std::cmp_less(-1, 1u) is true, as you would expect. There are also cmp_equal, cmp_greater and so on. It costs a couple of extra checks, so use it where mixing signs is unavoidable.

code.title: Fast I/O setup and parsing with from_chars

followUps:
It hangs because the program's prompt is still sitting in the output buffer, and the judge or user is waiting for it before sending the next input.

With cin.tie(nullptr) and no flush, cout only writes when its buffer fills or the program ends. The reader waits for a query, the program waits for the reply, and nobody moves. Fix: write cout << q << std::endl; or cout.flush() after every query. Use flushing only for interactive tasks.

Because eof() becomes true only after a read has already failed, so the loop runs one extra time with a stale or garbage value.

int x;
while (!cin.eof()) { cin >> x; sum += x; }  // wrong
while (cin >> x) sum += x;                // right

With the input "1 2" the wrong loop adds the last value twice (sum 5 instead of 3). Testing the read itself, as in while (cin >> x), is correct and also stops on bad input.

code.title: Why using namespace std is risky: name clashes

followUps:
A using-declaration brings in one name; a using-directive brings in every name from a namespace.

using std::cout; makes just cout usable unqualified. using namespace std; makes all of std visible for lookup, so a name like count or distance can become ambiguous with your own. The declaration is safer because you control exactly which names enter, and a clash with an existing name in the same scope is reported at once.

Mostly yes: using namespace std::literals; only exposes literal suffixes such as s, ms and sv, which are designed so they cannot clash with normal names.

Example: "hi"s is a std::string and 250ms is a std::chrono::milliseconds. Still keep it inside a function or .cpp file rather than in a header, so you do not push it onto every user of that header.

code.title: ADL and the swap idiom

followUps:
Yes, since C++20: ADL can find a function template even if you write explicit template arguments, as long as some template with that name is visible at that point.

Before C++20, f<int>(x) was parsed as a comparison unless a template named f was already visible by normal lookup, so ADL did not kick in. Example: get<0>(myTuple) relies on this for types in your own namespace. Explicit arguments still do not change which namespaces ADL searches.

A hidden friend is a friend function defined inside a class body, which can only be found through ADL and not through normal lookup.

struct Box {
    int w;
    friend void swap(Box& a, Box& b) { std::swap(a.w, b.w); }
};

Because it is invisible to ordinary lookup, it cannot clash with other overloads or be picked by accident; it is only considered when a Box is an argument. It is the recommended way to write operator<<, swap and comparison operators.

code.title: Static initialization order and construct on first use

followUps:
constinit guarantees that a variable with static or thread storage is initialized at compile time (constant initialization), so no dynamic initializer runs for it.

If the initializer is not a constant expression, the code does not compile. Unlike constexpr, the variable can still be modified later. Example: constinit int limit = compute(); only compiles if compute() is constexpr. That removes the init-order fiasco for that variable, because it is ready before any other code runs.

Because static objects are destroyed in reverse order of construction, a destructor may use another global that has already been destroyed.

Example: a global Logger is built after a global Cache; if Cache's destructor writes to the Logger, that is fine, but if the order is reversed the Logger is already gone, and the program touches a dead object (undefined behavior at exit). Across translation units the construction order is unspecified, so the destruction order is too. A function-local static (or an intentionally leaked object) avoids it.

code.title: Sharing config: inline variable, constexpr, accessor

followUps:
Protect it with a std::mutex (or make it std::atomic if it is a simple value), because an unprotected write racing with reads is undefined behavior.

std::atomic<int> maxConn{100};
maxConn.store(250);          // writer
int n = maxConn.load();      // reader

For a whole struct, hide it behind an accessor with a mutex, or publish a new immutable copy through std::shared_ptr so readers always see a consistent set of values.

Because a namespace-scope const variable has internal linkage by default, each .cpp that includes the header gets its own private copy and the linker never sees it.

That is why const int k = 5; in a header causes no multiple-definition error, while a non-const int k = 5; does. The default does not apply to extern const int k;, which has external linkage. For one shared object across files in C++17, use inline const int k = 5;.

code.title: Guarding against common undefined behavior

followUps:
Undefined behavior means the standard places no requirements at all on what happens; unspecified means a valid result from a set of options; implementation-defined means the compiler picks and documents it.

Examples: the order in which f(a(), b()) evaluates its arguments is unspecified (some order, no crash). The size of int is implementation-defined (documented per compiler). INT_MAX + 1 is undefined (anything may happen). Portable code can rely on unspecified results only if it works for every option.

Erroneous behavior (C++26) is a new category for mistakes like reading an uninitialized local variable: the program is wrong, but it is no longer undefined, so the compiler cannot assume it never happens.

Such reads give a fixed, implementation-chosen value instead of arbitrary results, and implementations are encouraged to report them (for example, by diagnostics or a trap). This keeps bugs detectable and limits damage, while still allowing [[indeterminate]] to opt out for performance-critical code.
